issues.issue: This says that under Option B the death benefit is decreased by the withdrawal and Withdrawal Charge "by the same amounts," which cannot be squared with §4.2 Coverage Option B, where the benefit is the greater of Specified Amount plus account value or the risk-percentage corridor amount. If the corridor branch controls, the benefit does not fall dollar-for-dollar as this provision states.

The six-month postponement of a withdrawal payment stands against §5.9's grant of the right to withdraw "at any time" and §4.1's payment undertaking. Which provision governs when the money must actually be paid is not stated.

Notice is to be mailed "at least 50 days before the end of the Grace Period," but §5.10's opening sentence makes the Grace Period only 60 days, so the notice duty would expire ten days into it. The two figures cannot comfortably be given effect together.

"[T]his Policy will terminate without value" cannot be squared with §3.4, which permits reinstatement within five years using the Policy Account Value, Indebtedness and Surrender Charges in effect when the Policy lapsed, nor with §5.6's state-law minimum Cash Value. Whether any value survives termination is left to construction.

"[A]ny premium which remains unpaid on the date of death" presupposes a premium that is due, but this is a flexible-premium policy under §3.2 in which no premium is ever owed after the first two years. What amount is deducted from the Proceeds on a grace-period death is therefore undefined.

The first-two-year no-lapse guarantee cannot be squared with §9.4, which states the Policy "will lapse whenever" Cash Value less indebtedness is insufficient for the next Monthly Insurance Charges, with no two-year carve-out. It also uses a different measure from §5.10's Surrender Value test.

Minimum values are said to rest on the mortality table and interest rate "specified by the laws of the state in which this Policy is delivered," and then a specific table and 4.5% rate are named. If the delivery state's law prescribes something different, the provision contradicts itself.

Increases are conditioned on "[a]n application satisfactory to us" and "[e]vidence of insurability satisfactory to us," standards the provision leaves entirely to the insurer's judgment with no stated benchmark. Whether that discretion is unlimited or bounded by reasonableness is the point of construction.

The effective date of an increase is stated only as "the Monthly Due Date following our [ap]proval," with the sentence broken across the promise to send "an addition to Section 1." When approval occurs, and whether the added Section 1 page or this sentence fixes the date, cannot be read off the text.

"We may limit the number of increases ... to no more than 1 in any period of 12 months" is permissive, so it is not stated whether the limit applies unless invoked or is a fixed cap. The word "may" leaves the owner unable to know how many increases are available.

This decrease provision omits any Minimum Specified Amount floor, while §5.9 expressly requires that the Specified Amount remaining after an Option A withdrawal be at least the Minimum Specified Amount shown in Section 1. Whether a requested decrease may take the Specified Amount below that floor turns on reading the two together.

The provision addresses only a change from Coverage Option A to Option B and is silent on a change from B to A, inviting an expressio unius argument that the reverse change is unavailable. The formula for the new Specified Amount ("the death benefit less the [Policy Account Value]") is also stated only in fragments.

"Any change to your Policy that is not provided for in this section" is ambiguous as to whether "this section" means §6.4 alone or all of Section 6, which changes the set of alterations requiring officer signature. The reach of the officer-signature requirement depends on which reading is taken.

"No agent has the authority to make any changes or waive any of the terms of your Policy" does not say whether it bars waiver or estoppel arising from the conduct of the writing agent named in Section 1, or only formal amendments. Its interaction with §6.4's officer-signature route leaves the scope of the bar open.

The entire-contract clause names only "[t]his Policy the application and any supplemental applications," omitting the attached riders that §2.7 and §5.5 treat as part of the coverage. Whether the Waiver of Deduction rider is part of the contract has to be decided against those provisions.

The bar on using unwritten statements, and the "in the absence of fraud" representations rule, must be read with §7.8's incontestability clause and its exception for insufficient Surrender Value. Whether a fraud-based contest survives the two-year period turns on how the two provisions fit together.

The provision makes the return-of-premium remedy "subject to Section 7.7 - Incontestability," but there is no §7.7 in this Policy; incontestability is §7.8. The misdirected cross-reference must be repaired before the limitation on liability can be applied.

The lapse-warning condition is ungrammatical as written — "when the Surrender Value together with interest at the guaranteed rate, deductions for the Monthly Insurance Charges at their guaranteed rates, will cause the Policy to lapse" — so the projection that triggers the notice is not stated. Whether the test uses guaranteed or current assumptions is left unclear.

The additional report is furnished "for a reasonable charge as determined by us," leaving reasonableness to the insurer's own determination with no benchmark. The clause also does not say how many additional reports may be requested.

The illustrative report is also priced at "a reasonable charge determined by us," an unbounded standard, and the sentence identifying what the projections are "based on information supplied i[n]" breaks off. The basis of the projections is therefore unstated.

The suicide exclusion runs "two years from the Issue Date," but "Issue Date" is nowhere defined in Section 2, which defines only Policy Date and Effective Date. Which date starts the two-year period is left to construction.

The incontestability promise is qualified by "unless the Surrender Value is insufficient to cover the next Monthly Cost of Insurance," an exception whose scope is unclear and which could swallow the rule for any lapsed or lapsing policy. It also measures the period from the undefined "Issue Date."

The reinstatement incontestability sentence does not say whether the preceding "unless the Surrender Value is insufficient" exception in §7.8 carries over to reinstatements, nor how it fits §3.4's five-year reinstatement right. The two sentences of §7.8 must be read together to fix the insurer's contest rights.

The increase-contestability sentence omits the qualifier attached to the Initial Specified Amount sentence of §7.8 and does not identify the date from which the two years run for an increase. Its relation to §6.2's effective date of increase has to be worked out.

Conditioning the Owner's exercise of "every right provided by your Policy" on there being no assignment cannot be squared with §8.3, which contemplates assignment while leaving the Owner rights subject to it, or with §5.8's right to surrender "at any time." What rights survive an assignment is unresolved between the two.

The change of ownership is "effective [as of the date the] request was signed" yet has "no effect on any payment made or other action taken by us" before receipt, so the change is both retroactive and not. Which owner is entitled to a payment made in the interval is left ambiguous.

The clause subordinates "[y]our rights and the rights of any revocable beneficiary" to an assignment, saying nothing about an irrevocable beneficiary, inviting the inference that such a beneficiary's rights are not subordinated. That silence controls whether an assignment binds an irrevocable beneficiary.

The beneficiary is fixed by "the application," while Section 1 of the Policy states "BENEFICIARY: AS SPECIFIED ON THE" application and §2.4 makes it the person named in the original application subject to change. Which writing establishes the beneficiary of record must be settled across those provisions.

The predecease rules address only beneficiaries who die "before the Insured" and provide nothing for a beneficiary who dies simultaneously with the Insured or after death but before payment. That gap determines who takes the death proceeds in those cases.

A beneficiary change is "effective upon the date your request was signed" but has "no effect on any payment made or other action taken by us before we receive it," so the change is simultaneously retroactive and ineffective. Whether an unreceived signed change defeats a payment already made is the point of doubt.

The loan grant survives only as a fragment ("You may obtain a Policy [loan] ... us is the only security needed"), so the conditions on which a loan may be taken are not stated in the provision. Its terms have to be supplied from §9.2 and §9.3.
The provision states the deductions from the loan available but never states the base amount from which they are subtracted. Without that base the maximum loan cannot be computed from the text.

Loan interest is charged "at the rate specified in Section [1]," the same Policy Loan Interest Rate that §5.2 uses (less two points) to credit interest on the loaned account value with an arithmetically erroneous illustration. The net cost of a loan depends on reconciling this provision with §5.2.

Indebtedness is deducted here "from the Policy Proceeds," while §4.2 provides that death benefits "will be decreased by the amount of any indebtedness under the Policy on the date of death." The two use different bases and, read literally, could deduct the same debt twice.

This lapse trigger — "whenever the excess of the Cash Value over the total Policy Indebtedness is not sufficient" — differs from §5.10, which measures Surrender Value on a Monthly Due Date and grants a 60-day Grace Period, and it makes no mention of that Grace Period or of §5.10's first-two-year no-lapse protection. Which provision governs when the Policy lapses is squarely in issue.

The payee's election right is stated in scrambled fragments and made "subject to Section 8," leaving unclear whether the Owner, the Insured, or the Beneficiary elects in a given case. Section 8's ownership and beneficiary rules must be consulted to identify the electing party.

The installment option's text is internally incoherent — payments "either for a specified period or for a specified amount, the present value, which is equal to the Policy Proceeds" — so how the payment amount or duration is fixed cannot be determined. The 4% floor sits in the same broken sentence.

The guaranteed life-income figures recited here for a male payee age 65 ($6.77 per $1,000, and the figure given for the guaranteed-period form) do not match the Payments for Life Table later in Section 10, which shows 6.72 and 6.62 for age 65. A court would have to decide whether the text or the table states the guarantee.

The joint life income option states that "[g]uaranteed rates will be furnished upon request," supplying no guaranteed minimum in the Policy itself, unlike Options 2 and 3 which carry tables. The minimum payable under this option is therefore not ascertainable from the contract.

The withdrawal restriction is stated in a broken clause ("unless the B[eneficiary] Designation limits withdrawals, any withdrawal must ..."), so both the restriction and any minimum withdrawal amount are indeterminate. Whether a beneficiary designation can bind the payee's withdrawal right is left unclear.

Determining all option amounts "using our rates in effect at the time of settlement" cannot be squared with the guaranteed minimums stated in Option 2 (never less than 4%), Option 3 (never less than the guaranteed rates) and Option 5 (at least 4%). Which controls when current rates fall below the guarantees is the question.

The elective guaranteed periods are garbled ("not less than % 10, Ss, -or 20 years"), so the certain periods actually available cannot be read from the provision, and the table columns list five such periods. Option 3's text also refers to a guaranteed minimum period without matching this list.
